intro: This annex classifies every district of Punjab, Sindh, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan as predominantly urban, mixed or peri-urban, or predominantly rural, using the 7th Population and Housing Census 2023 of the Pakistan Bureau of Statistics (PBS). It supports the geography layer of the segmentation framework (Section 3.1b) and the selection of urban and rural tehsils for the rapid baseline assessment (Section 3.1a). District figures are aggregated from PBS tehsil-level tables (Table 1: area, population and urban population; Table 12: literacy of the population aged 10 and above).
province_source: Source: PBS, 7th Population and Housing Census 2023, Tables 1 and 12; provincial totals are sums of district rows. PBS's household summary gives Sindh 53.73% urban and Pakistan 38.82% urban.

Punjab: 59% of the population lives in rural areas. Female literacy is 74.0% in urban areas and 50.5% in rural areas, a gap of 23.5 points.

Female literacy is lowest in the south-western riverine and agricultural districts (Rajanpur 28.2%, Dera Ghazi Khan 37.2%, Muzaffargarh 39.7%, Rahim Yar Khan 40.2%) and highest in Rawalpindi, Gujrat and Lahore (77–78%). Southern districts are under 27% urban and need low-literacy, voice and visual content.

14 of 36 census districts are predominantly rural and 19 are mixed, typically a district town surrounded by canal-colony villages. Peri-urban belts around Lahore, Faisalabad, Gujranwala, Sialkot and Multan have relatively good phone and agent coverage.
Sindh: The seven Karachi districts hold 20.4 million people, 62.8% of Sindh's urban population. Outside Karachi Division, Sindh is only 31.7% urban.

Sindh has the widest rural–urban gap for women: female literacy is 67.8% in urban areas and 27.5% in rural areas. It is lowest in the coastal and desert districts (Sujawal 19.7%, Thatta 20.1%, Tharparkar 23.5%, Tando Muhammad Khan 25.0%).
Only 33.1% of women aged 15–49 own a mobile phone, against 81.4% of men (Sindh MICS 2018–19).
Rural Sindh combines irrigated agriculture, riverine katcha areas and the Thar desert; women work mostly in unpaid farm and livestock activity with limited mobility.
Khyber Pakhtunkhwa: The most rural province: 33 of 35 census districts are predominantly rural and 12 recorded no urban population (including Bajaur, Mohmand, Orakzai, South Waziristan, Batagram, Buner, Shangla, Torghar, the three Kohistan districts and Upper Chitral). Only Peshawar (40.1%) and Swat (29.6%) are mixed.
Female literacy is 55.4% in urban and 33.8% in rural areas, falling to 10–15% in the Kohistan belt and merged districts (Upper and Lower Kohistan 10.3%, Bajaur 12.3%, Torghar 12.5%).
Only 34.6% of women aged 15–49 own a mobile phone, against 87.1% of men (KP MICS 2019), so shared household handsets are the norm.
Mountainous and merged districts have scattered settlements, patchy connectivity, few agents and strong restrictions on women's mobility.
Balochistan: Balochistan covers 44% of Pakistan's area with 6% of its population; density is 42.9 persons per km² and about 6 in Chagai and Awaran. 19 of 34 districts are predominantly rural; only Quetta (60.3%) and Gwadar (52.1%) are predominantly urban.
Female literacy is 46.5% in urban and 26.6% in rural areas, lowest in Dera Bugti (11.9%), Sherani (15.0%) and Washuk (15.8%).
30.1% of women aged 15–49 own a mobile phone, the lowest among the provinces (Balochistan MICS 2019–20).

Distinct district types: the flood-prone canal-irrigated rice belt in the east (Nasirabad, Jaffarabad, Sohbatpur), the highland orchard districts around Quetta, the Makran coast and date belt (Gwadar, Kech, Panjgur), and vast desert and mining districts (Chagai, Washuk, Kharan).

sources: Pakistan Bureau of Statistics (2024). 7th Population and Housing Census 2023: Detailed Results, Table 1 (area, population, urban proportion) and Table 12 (literacy by sex and rural/urban). post_census_note: Districts notified after the census (Murree, Talagang, Wazirabad, Kot Addu and Taunsa in Punjab; Hub and Usta Muhammad in Balochistan; Upper and Lower South Waziristan in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa) are not separate census districts. Their figures below are sums of their PBS tehsil rows and are already included in the parent district rows above.
